title: Which relative? ({qui}, {que}, {où}, {dont}, {ce qui}, {ce que})
description: Put {qui}, {que}, {où}, {dont}, {ce qui} and {ce que} in one table, and pick each one by what follows it.
can_do: Pick the word that joins a second idea to a noun: {le monsieur qui habite à côté}, {la piscine où Noé nage}, {le pote dont je t'ai parlé}
Say what you mean without naming the thing: {Je fais ce que je veux.} {Tu sais ce qui est drôle ?}
line: Choose the word by what follows the noun: a verb takes {qui}, a new subject takes {que}, a place or a time takes {où}, a word used with {de} takes {dont}, and with no noun you say {ce qui} or {ce que}.

parts.heading: Each word and what follows it
text: Each of these words adds a second idea to a noun, so you can say which person, thing, place or day you mean. To pick one, look at the noun and at what comes right after it.

rows.sub: the noun is a place or a time

rows.fr: le quartier dont je suis fière

rows.sub: no noun, and a verb comes next
no noun, and a new subject comes next

parts.heading: {qui} or {que}: a verb or a new subject
text: In questions, {qui est-ce qui} asks who does the action and {qui est-ce que} asks who receives it. After a noun the split is the same. {qui} means the noun does the action, so the verb comes next. {que} means the noun receives the action, so a new subject comes next, such as {je}, {tu} or {on}.
parts.note: {que} becomes {qu'} before a vowel: {le livre qu'elle lit}. {qui} never shortens: {la voisine qui a un chien}.

pairs: le monsieur qui habite à côté
the man who lives next door
la voisine qui a un chien
the neighbour who has a dog
Maya, c'est la copine que j'invite samedi.
Maya is the friend I'm inviting on Saturday.

parts.heading: {où}: a place or a time
text: After a place or a day, {où} says what happens there or then. A new subject often comes next, as it does after {que}, but the noun is a place or a time, so the word is {où}.
parts.note: {où} with an accent means where or when. {ou} without one means or.

lines: la boulangerie où je vais tous les matins
the bakery I go to every morning
le jour où Maya est arrivée

parts.heading: {dont}: words used with {de}
text: Some words are used with {de}: {parler de}, {être fier de}. With them, {dont} stands for {de} and the noun together, so no {de} comes after it.

build.fr: Je suis fière de ce quartier.
C'est un quartier dont je suis fière.
build.en: It's a neighbourhood I'm proud of.

build.fr: Hugo, c'est le pote dont je t'ai parlé.
build.en: Hugo is the mate I told you about.

parts.heading: {ce qui} and {ce que}: no noun
text: When you do not name the thing first, {ce} takes the place of the noun, and the English is usually what. The same split holds: a verb next takes {ce qui}, a new subject next takes {ce que}.

lines: Tu sais ce qui est drôle ?
Je fais ce que je veux.
Dis-moi ce que tu aimes ici.
Tell me what you like here.

checks.ask: Léa shows Maya round. Which word fills the gap? «C'est la piscine ___ Noé nage le samedi.»
checks.why: A new subject comes next, {Noé}, but the noun is a place, so the word is {où}: Noé swims there.

checks.ask: Which one says “Hugo is the mate I told you about”?

options.text: Hugo, c'est le pote que je t'ai parlé.
Hugo, c'est le pote dont je t'ai parlé.
Hugo, c'est le pote qui je t'ai parlé.

checks.why: You talk about someone with {parler de}, so the word is {dont}. It stands for {de Hugo}.

checks.ask: Léa tells Maya she is free on Saturday. Which words fill the gap? «Samedi, je fais ___ je veux.»
checks.why: There is no noun, so the gap starts with {ce}. A new subject comes next, {je}, so it is {ce que}.
